title: NASA's Chief Just Offered to Help India Build Its Own Space Station. India Hasn't Said Yes.
excerpt: Bill Nelson's India visit confirms an ISRO astronaut will fly to the ISS by 2027. The bigger question is whether New Delhi wants American help on the station it plans to build by 2035.
body:
NASA Administrator Bill Nelson landed in India this week with an offer that would have seemed unthinkable a decade ago: help building an Indian space station.

Speaking in New Delhi, Nelson confirmed that the United States and India are working on plans to send an ISRO-selected astronaut to the International Space Station by the end of 2027 — a mission that would make India only the fourth country to put its own astronaut aboard the station through a bilateral agreement.

"The selection of astronaut is determined by ISRO. NASA will not make the selection," Nelson said, underscoring that the collaboration is structured as a partnership between equals, not a favour.

## The Space Station Question

But it was his next remark that carried the real weight. When asked whether NASA would collaborate with India on its planned space station, Nelson was unequivocal.

"We expect by that time to have a commercial space station. I think India wants to have a commercial space station by 2040. If India wants us to collaborate with them, of course, we will be available. But that's up to India."

The phrasing was deliberate. India has not formally requested American assistance on its space station programme. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has set ISRO a target of building an Indian space station by 2035 and landing astronauts on the moon by 2040 — timelines that suggest New Delhi wants to develop indigenous capability first, even if it takes longer.

ISRO's Gaganyaan programme, which will put Indian astronauts in low-Earth orbit, has completed two uncrewed test flights this year. The agency is preparing for at least one more before a crewed mission, now expected in 2027.

## A Full Dance Card

Nelson's India visit is packed. He met Science and Technology Minister Jitendra Singh in New Delhi, is scheduled to meet space-sector business leaders in Mumbai, and will visit ISRO headquarters in Bengaluru — where he plans to meet Rakesh Sharma, the first and so far only Indian citizen to fly in space, who went to orbit aboard a Soviet Soyuz in 1984.

The visit builds on the Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology (iCET) framework, launched by Modi and then-President Joe Biden, which placed space at the centre of the bilateral technology relationship. Under that agreement, ISRO astronauts are being trained at NASA's Johnson Space Center, and the jointly developed NISAR Earth-observation satellite — capable of mapping the planet's entire surface every 12 days — has been operational since its launch earlier this year.

## What It Means for India's Commercial Space Sector

The timing matters. India's private space sector has grown rapidly, with startups like Skyroot Aerospace and Agnikul Cosmos developing their own launch vehicles, and companies like Pixxel and Dhruva Space building satellite constellations. American investment has followed: Amazon's $48 billion India commitment announced this week includes cloud infrastructure that space companies will rely on for satellite data processing.

A deeper NASA-ISRO partnership could open doors for Indian space startups seeking contracts with American agencies — much as Israeli and Japanese firms have benefited from their countries' space agreements with the US.

## The Diaspora Connection

The partnership also reflects the growing influence of Indian-origin scientists and engineers in America's space programme. NASA astronaut Sunita Williams has completed multiple ISS missions, and the agency's ranks include thousands of Indian-American engineers and researchers. The upcoming ISRO astronaut mission to the ISS would add a new chapter to a relationship that has been building from both ends — Indian talent shaping American space exploration, and American collaboration accelerating India's own ambitions.

Nelson, 83, has been NASA administrator since 2021 and is himself a former astronaut who flew on the Space Shuttle Columbia in 1986. His visit to India — his second as administrator — signals that the US views space as one of the most productive arenas for the bilateral relationship, even as trade and immigration tensions simmer elsewhere.

"There is so much that India and the US can do together," Nelson said. For now, the ball is in ISRO's court.

*Sources: The Indian Eye, NASA, Reuters, Indian News Network, Observer Research Foundation*
